segments.name: Opening: The World of Bleak House

passages.summary: Mr. Guppy and his friend quickly tire, showing disinterest and fatigue as they tour successive rooms of Dedlock portraits while Mrs. Rouncewell maintains dignified approval.
passages.best_quote: whose family greatness seems to consist in their never having done anything to distinguish themselves for seven hundred years

passages.summary: Esther describes waking before dawn and watching the landscape gradually emerge from darkness and mist, comparing the process to how memory reveals one's past.
passages.best_quote: like my memory over my life

passages.summary: Mr. Jarndyce addresses Richard and Ada, confirming he is glad to have their confidence and that he did contemplate their union as a possibility.
passages.best_quote: When I contemplated these relations between us four which have so brightened my life and so invested it with new interests and pleasures, I certainly did contemplate, afar off, the possibility of you and your pretty cousin here (don't be shy, Ada, don't be shy, my dear!) being in a mind to go through life together. I saw, and do see, many reasons to make it desirable. But that was afar off, Rick, afar off!

passages.summary: Mr. Jarndyce counsels Ada and Richard that while he assumes their love will endure, if they change he will remain their confidant and will not judge them.
passages.best_quote: I will assume that a few years hence you will be in your hearts to one another what you are to-day. All I say before speaking to you according to that assumption is, if you DO change—if you DO come to find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and woman than you were as boy and girl (your manhood will excuse me, Rick!)—don't be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be nothing monstrous or uncommon in it.

passages.summary: Mr. Jarndyce advises Richard to trust Providence and his own efforts equally, to combine constancy in love with diligent effort in all pursuits, and never to expect success without genuine commitment.
passages.best_quote: Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner. Constancy in love is a good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy in every kind of effort. If you had the abilities of all the great men, past and present, you could do nothing well without sincerely meaning it and setting about it.

passages.summary: As Ada and Richard leave, Esther observes them passing through sunlit rooms, young and full of hope, but the sun clouds over as they depart, suggesting a foreboding shadow.
passages.best_quote: So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come and making them all years of brightness. So they passed away into the shadow and were gone. It was only a burst of light that had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over.

passages.summary: Richard and Ada confide to Esther their mutual love, placing themselves on either side of her. Esther counsels them about the demands of enduring love and promises to speak to Mr. Jarndyce.
passages.best_quote: They went on in their own wild way for a little while—I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself—and then we gradually fell to considering how young they were, and how there must be a lapse of several years before this early love could come to anything, and how it could come to happiness only if it were real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and perseverance, each always for the other's sake.

passages.summary: Mrs. Badger elaborates that Richard lacks the positive interest in medicine that sustains practitioners through hardship, unlike Mr. Woodcourt whose commitment comes from genuine passion.
passages.best_quote: Young men like Mr. Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a very little money and through years of considerable endurance and disappointment.

passages.summary: Mrs. Piper testifies ramblingly about neighborhood rumors of the dead man's depravity and dangerous temperament toward children.
passages.best_quote: the plaintive—so Mrs. Piper insists on calling the deceased—was reported to have sold himself.

passages.summary: Jo testifies to his name, complete social isolation, illiteracy, and basic moral beliefs despite having no formal education.
passages.best_quote: No father, no mother, no friends. Never been to school.

passages.summary: Jo reveals the dead man recognized him, showed him kindness, asked about his welfare, and when poor himself, shared what little he had.
passages.best_quote: Neither have I. Not one! and gave him the price of a supper and a night's lodging.

passages.summary: Mr. Guppy warns that the letters thought destroyed are likely being used as material for blackmail, with visitors present this morning to extract payment.
passages.best_quote: That the visitors I have alluded to have been here this morning to make money of it. And that the money is made, or making.

passages.summary: Mr. Kenge defends the expenditure of great legal talent on Jarndyce and Jarndyce, arguing that the public and country benefit from such intellectual engagement.
passages.best_quote: the flower of the bar, and the—a—I would presume to add, the matured autumnal fruits of the woolsack

passages.summary: Sir Leicester slowly reads Mr. Tulkinghorn's message stating that he has discovered the identity and location of the man who copied the affidavit Lady Dedlock inquired about.
passages.best_quote: I have something to tell her on her return in reference to the person who copied the affidavit in the Chancery suit, which so powerfully stimulated her curiosity. I have seen him.

passages.summary: Throughout the exchange, Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn watch each other intently while maintaining composure; Sir Leicester watches the fire. The narrative reveals their mutual suspicion and hidden knowledge.
passages.best_quote: During the utterance of every word of this short dialogue, Lady Dedlock and Mr. Tulkinghorn, without any other alteration in their customary deportment, have looked very steadily at one another—as was natural, perhaps, in the discussion of so unusual a subject...But whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares; what each would give to know how much the other knows—all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts.

passages.summary: The passage describes the subsequent meetings of Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn at Chesney Wold; they maintain their social masks while watchfully observing each other, each suspicious of the other's hidden knowledge and prepared for revelation.
passages.best_quote: They meet again at dinner—again, next day—again, for many days in succession. Lady Dedlock is always the same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine. Mr. Tulkinghorn is always the same speechless repository of noble confidences, so oddly out of place and yet so perfectly at home...But whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares; what each would give to know how much the other knows—all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts.

passages.summary: At sunset, Tulkinghorn finally appears, moving at his usual methodical pace with an expressionless mask, embodying mystery and unknown knowledge.
passages.best_quote: He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress. Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his personal secret. He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients; he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself.

passages.summary: Mr. Jarndyce explains that the lady, who claims to be Esther's aunt, has maintained absolute secrecy about her identity and refused to provide any further information despite Mr. Kenge's mediation.
passages.best_quote: That she was, if there were any ties of blood in such a case, the child's aunt. That more than this she would never (and he was well persuaded of the steadfastness of her resolution) for any human consideration disclose.

passages.summary: Dickens recounts a Chancery judge's claim that the Court of Chancery is nearly perfect, attributing its minor delays to the public's parsimony in funding judicial positions.
passages.best_quote: the Court of Chancery, though the shining subject of much popular prejudice, was almost immaculate

passages.summary: The woman reveals she was also once a Chancery ward; her youth, hope, and beauty did not save her, and she still waits for judgment in Chancery.
passages.best_quote: Neither of the three served or saved me. I have the honour to attend court regularly. With my documents. I expect a judgment. Shortly. On the Day of Judgment.

passages.summary: Richard appears at the door and jokingly warns Esther not to let Krook buy her hair.
passages.best_quote: Miss Summerson, I hope you are not bargaining for the sale of your hair. Don't be tempted. Three sacks below are quite enough for Mr. Krook!

passages.summary: The cottage contains a bruised woman with a dying baby, a dissipated man smoking on the floor, a young man with a dog, and a girl washing in filthy water.
passages.best_quote: Besides ourselves, there were in this damp, offensive room a woman with a black eye, nursing a poor little gasping baby by the fire; a man, all stained with clay and mud and looking very dissipated, lying at full length on the ground, smoking a pipe; a powerful young man fastening a collar on a dog; and a bold girl doing some kind of washing in very dirty water.

passages.summary: The narrator directly addresses Jo, acknowledging his legal rejection but affirming that his love for the dead man is a form of grace and light.
passages.best_quote: There is something like a distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: 'He wos wery good to me, he wos!'

segments.name: Closing: What Bleak House Means Today

passages.summary: Despite his fierce words, Boythorn treats the ladies with great gentleness and propriety.
Lady Dedlock has made a definitive decision about something discussed with Tulkinghorn and is prepared to act.
Jarndyce formally presents Esther as a gift to Woodcourt, praising her as the best wife and acknowledging Woodcourt's worthiness.
passages.best_quote: Allan, take from me a willing gift, the best wife that ever man had. What more can I say for you than that I know you deserve her!
